title: Gains and Collapse in On-Policy Distillation: A Reinforcement Learning Perspective

paper.title:
Gains and Collapse in On-Policy Distillation:
A Reinforcement Learning Perspective
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) has become an important approach to language model post-training.
However, despite its performance gains, OPD can also collapse into excessively long and repetitive generation, and the mechanism underlying these divergent outcomes remains poorly understood.
We explain these outcomes through a reinforcement learning perspective: the teacher implicitly rewards student behaviors, even those it rarely exhibits itself.
From this perspective, our experiments show that OPD improves performance without expanding the student’s capabilities.
When the implicit reward model is reliable, OPD makes correct responses easier to sample.
In contrast, when the preference misaligns with quality, reward hacking happens:
the implicit reward model amplifies overlong, repetitive student rollouts, even though it rarely generates such text itself.
Guided by this diagnosis, we find that masking unhealthy responses during training and using SFT initialization can each effectively mitigate the collapse.
Together, these findings show that OPD amplifies student behaviors favored by the teacher’s implicit feedback, shifting the focus from how well the teacher generates to how reliably it evaluates student rollouts.
Our code is available at https://github.com/HancCui/opd_hacking .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become an important approach for developing frontier language models and has been adopted in large-scale post-training pipelines ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ; Kimi Team et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . At each iteration, the current student samples its own responses, and the teacher supervises it through token-level KL divergence at student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . While prior work has demonstrated the potential of OPD to improve student performance, recent studies have reported unstable training and degenerate behaviors, including excessive response length and repetition ( Li et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . It remains unclear what OPD actually learns during training, and why this learning process can sometimes lead to collapse. In this paper, we view OPD from an RL perspective, in which the teacher implicitly rewards the student’s own responses. We investigate OPD on mathematical tasks using different types of teachers, including RL-trained reasoning models and larger general-purpose models. Our experiments show that OPD does not directly extend the student’s capability. Instead, it changes the relative probability of responses the student already produces according to the teacher’s preferences. When these preferences align with response quality, this reweighting can improve sampling efficiency; when they do not, it can lead to reward hacking, with the student increasingly producing responses that receive high implicit rewards despite poor quality. We substantiate this view through three findings. First, we show that successful OPD reinforces correct responses the student can already generate. We compare the initial and trained students across sampling budgets, combining pass@ k k evaluation with additional sampling and manual audits. Although OPD substantially improves single-sample accuracy(pass@1), the gains progressively diminish as the sampling budget increases. At the same time, we find no expansion of the observed solvable set: problems solved after OPD can also be solved by the initial student given sufficient sampling. Together, these results suggest that OPD makes existing capabilities easier to elicit rather than expanding the student model’s problem-solving capabilities. In contrast, we find that the observed OPD collapse reflects reward hacking: training reinforces poor-quality responses favored by the teacher. We compare a successful OPD run with a reproduction of the collapsed setting reported by Li et al. (2026) . Despite their sharply different outcomes, both runs converge normally and concentrate on responses with low negative log-likelihood under the initial student, suggesting that collapse is not simply a failure of optimization or convergence. In the collapsed run, the student produces increasingly overlong and repetitive responses. At the same time, its response distribution shifts markedly toward responses preferred by the teacher over those the teacher disfavors, indicating that the student is fitting the teacher’s preference signal increasingly well. The student thus learns the teacher’s preferences even as its generation quality deteriorates. Building on this diagnosis, we mitigate OPD collapse with a standard remedy for reward hacking: limiting the reinforcement of pathological responses. Before training, higher implicit rewards favor correct and concise responses in the successful setting, but overlong and repetitive responses in the collapsed setting, with both types of behavior later amplified during training. Notably, the teacher itself rarely generates such pathological responses, showing that generation quality does not reliably reflect feedback quality on student rollouts. Keeping the teacher fixed, masking rollouts that reach the generation limit mitigates degeneration and improves average evaluation accuracy by 3.08 percentage points, and SFT warmup provides a complementary solution by improving the quality of the student’s initial rollout distribution. Together, these results show that collapse can be mitigated by controlling which student rollouts are available for reinforcement. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We interpret OPD as an RL-like process with the teacher acting as an implicit reward model, linking its performance gains to improved sampling efficiency. • We identify reward hacking in the observed collapse: the student fits the teacher’s preferences increasingly well even as its generation quality deteriorates. • We trace the collapse to a biased teacher reward signal. Limiting the reinforcement of this biased signal through masking, or reducing exposure to pathological rollouts through SFT warmup, mitigates collapse.

sections.heading: 2 On-policy distillation as implicit reward optimization
sections.text: We formulate the sampled-token reverse-KL variant of on-policy distillation (OPD) studied in this paper as policy optimization with a teacher-derived reward. This formulation makes explicit what the teacher scores, how those scores guide student updates, and why their reliability must be examined on student-generated trajectories.

sections.heading: 2.3 Experimental settings
sections.text: We study three teacher–student settings, summarized in Table 1 . The JustRL and DeepScaleR settings share the same student initialization and training data. Their teachers, JustRL-1.5B ( He et al., 2025 ) and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , were obtained through RL from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , which also initializes our student. Both settings use the level ≥ 6 \geq 6 subset of DeepMath-103K and a 16,384-token rollout limit. The Qwen3-4B setting follows Li et al. (2026) , using Qwen3-4B to supervise Qwen3-1.7B-Base on OpenThoughts3 prompts ( Guha et al., 2025 ) with an 8,192-token rollout limit. The teacher remains fixed in all settings. We train for 100 rollout iterations using the Slime training framework ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , with a reference-KL coefficient of 0.001 0.001 . We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME24–26, reporting mean@4 for routine evaluation and using 256 responses per problem for the coverage and sampling efficiency analyses. Full training and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 3 Does OPD Expand Student’s Capability Boundary?
sections.text: The implicit-reward perspective suggests that successful OPD can improve performance by reinforcing correct student responses. We examine this successful case: does teacher feedback make problems already solvable by the initial student easier to solve? We compare the initial student S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} with the trained student S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} using pass ​ @ ​ k \mathrm{pass}@k across increasing sampling budgets, audited problem coverage, and per-problem success rates.

For each of these problems, we draw 768 additional responses from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} , bringing its pool to 1024 responses. After additional sampling and manual review, no problem remains solved only by S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} : candidate cases are resolved either by finding a valid S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} solution or by excluding an invalid S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} derivation. The audited S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} set contains 73 solvable problems, against which S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} covers 65 under JustRL-1.5B and 63 under DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview. These indicate that OPD does not induce an observed expansion of the solvable set.

sections.heading: Already-solvable problems become easier to solve.

OPD raises success rates on problems already solvable by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} . The dashed line marks equal score. To identify the source of OPD’s small- k k gains, we compare per-problem success rates between S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} and S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} . For each problem q q , let p ^ m ​ ( q ) \hat{p}_{m}(q) denote the fraction of correct responses among the 256 samples from model m m . As shown in Figure 4 , the problem-level distribution is strongly shifted above the diagonal under both teachers. OPD increases the per-problem success rate for 90.6% of the problems already solvable by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} with JustRL-1.5B as the teacher, and for 84.4% with DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview. Averaged over these problems, the increase in mean@256 is 22.6% and 14.7%, respectively. Problems unimproved by OPD are those that S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} could hardly solve, and no high-performing problem drops to near-zero accuracy (lower-right corner). Some even jump from low to high success rates (upper-left corner), showing that OPD can make problems the initial student rarely solves much easier to solve. Thus, OPD primarily eases sampling of correct answers on already-solvable problems, which accounts for the small-k performance gain.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: In the two successful settings studied here, OPD improves sampling efficiency on problems already solvable by the initial student. Its positive accuracy gains disappear at the largest sampling budgets tested, and no validated OPD-only problem remains after the targeted AIME coverage audit. These findings are consistent with the teacher acting as an implicit reward model whose feedback reinforces correct student behavior, making successful responses easier to sample.

sections.heading: 4 Reward Hacking in OPD: Convergence to a Biased Reward Signal
sections.text: Figure 5 : Training process of the JustRL (top) and Qwen3-4B (bottom) settings. Optimization converges normally in both settings, and the trained student’s responses remain highly likely under S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} . Columns: the advantage and training loss; the Min-10NN distance over six checkpoints; the NLL under S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} of responses from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} and S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} . The preceding analysis shows that OPD improves performance without expanding the set of problems the student can solve. Yet OPD training does not always succeed: some teacher-student pairs produce collapsed behaviors instead. From a diagnostic perspective, we then examine whether the collapse constitutes reward hacking: optimization succeeding at the wrong target. We first verify that the optimization converges normally, then characterize the behavioral shifts that emerge during training.

sections.heading: 4.1 Collapsed OPD Training Still Converges Normally
sections.text: Our analysis starts by comparing a reported failure case of OPD with a successful one. Prior work ( Li et al., 2026 ) reports that OPD can fail when the teacher and student distributions are substantially mismatched, attributing the resulting degradation to this large distribution gap. We therefore compare the full training process of the two settings: the JustRL setting (JustRL-1.5B → \rightarrow DS-Distill-1.5B) where training improves the student, and the Qwen3-4B setting (Qwen3-4B → \rightarrow Qwen3-1.7B-Base, without warm-up) where training collapses. The loss and advantage in the Qwen3-4B setting converge as smoothly as those in the JustRL setting, with no qualitative difference in the shape of the curves. We measure response concentration using the Min-10NN distance ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which averages the ten smallest nearest-neighbor distances among responses to the same problem; lower values indicate greater similarity (described in detail in Appendix C ). The distance keeps decreasing during training in both settings: mildly in the JustRL setting, and much more sharply in the Qwen3-4B one. Both students shrink toward a narrower space of behaviors, a phenomenon also reported in other work on on-policy RLVR post-training ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Dang et al., 2025 ) . If training exploits the reward rather than learning from it, the selected behaviors should already be accessible to S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} rather than genuinely novel. To examine this, we compute the NLL under S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} for responses generated by the trained student and compare it with the NLL of S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} ’s own responses to the same problems. Figure 5 summarizes these diagnostics; the right panel reports this NLL comparison. In both settings, the trained student’s responses lie in the low NLL region of S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} , which indicates that they are already familiar to S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} .

sections.heading: 5 Diagnosing and Mitigating Reward Hacking
sections.text: To address reward hacking, prior work identifies which training samples exploit the reward model, then removes or reweights them during optimization ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Beigi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Following this strategy, we first diagnose which S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses the teacher assigns high advantage to, then test whether masking pathological responses or reinitializing from a cleaner distribution can prevent the collapse.

sections.heading: 5.1 The Teacher’s Reward Signal Can Be Misaligned with Response Quality
sections.text: Figure 7 : Teacher advantage over S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses from A1 (lowest advantage) to A10 (highest advantage). The JustRL teacher (top) assigns higher advantage to correct and shorter responses; the Qwen3-4B teacher (bottom) assigns higher advantage to overlong, repetitive ones. Dashed lines mark the teacher’s own mean length. To characterize the responses favored by the teacher before training, we rank all sampled S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses by their mean teacher advantage and divide them into ten equally sized groups, A1–A10. Each group contains 10% of the responses, with A1 containing the lowest-advantage responses and A10 the highest. Figure 7 reports correctness, response length, generation-cap hit rate, and severe-repetition rate across advantage deciles. In the JustRL setting, teacher advantage is aligned with response quality: correctness increases toward A10, response length decreases toward the teacher’s own average, and no severe repetition is detected. The Qwen3-4B setting shows the opposite pattern. The highest-advantage responses are not the most reliable ones: their correctness remains close to zero, whereas their length, truncation rate, and repetition rate increase substantially across advantage deciles. Although these pathological responses are rare under S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} , the teacher assigns them high advantage, causing OPD to amplify them during training. We also find similar failure pattern when the teacher is replaced as Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Appendix E presents three high-advantage S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses that exhibit excessive length and mechanical repetition. Figure 8 : Student-rollout characteristics during training. All the masking settings recover from the collapse, whereas Qwen3-4B-warmup avoids it from the beginning.

This suggests that the collapse may depend on which responses are supplied to the teacher for supervision. To test this hypothesis, we intervene on the candidate pool in the Qwen3-4B setting while keeping the teacher, training data, and optimization recipe fixed. We consider two interventions: (1) The Qwen3-4B-masked setting : masking the loss on responses that reach the generation length limit. (2) The Qwen3-4B-warmup setting : changing only the student initialization, from Qwen3-1.7B-Base to an SFT-initialized student released by Li et al. (2026) . Appendix F provides the training details for both interventions. 2 2 footnotetext: Warmup uses the Qwen3-1.7B-SFT checkpoint released by Li et al. (2026) . Masking recovers from collapse, while warmup avoids it. Figure 8 shows how response length, truncation, and repetition evolve over the course of training. The original Qwen3-4B setting eventually enters a persistent collapsed state, where responses become increasingly long, truncated, and repetitive. For the Qwen3-4B-masked setting, the student model exhibits few abnormal behaviors in the early training phase, so its learning trajectory closely aligns with that of the original Qwen3-4B. As the undesirable behaviors accumulate, the effect of the masking intervention becomes clear: the Qwen3-4B-masked setting recovers, while the original setting collapses. On the other hand, the warmup setting never develops this failure mode. Warmup has been adopted as a remedy for OPD collapse ( Li et al., 2026 ) . The SFT-initialized student rarely produces the pathological responses favored by the teacher, leaving fewer such responses for OPD to reinforce. Together, these results suggest that the collapse is not irreversible; it depends on whether abnormal responses continue to receive reinforcement during training. Both interventions improve final accuracy. Table 3 extends the accuracy comparison to Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B teachers. Masking improves the average accuracy over AMC23 and AIME24–26 by 3.08, 0.51, and 2.58 percentage points for the 4B, 8B, and 30B-A3B teachers, respectively. These gains are not uniform across benchmarks: with the 8B teacher, AIME24 accuracy is unchanged while AIME25 and AIME26 accuracy decrease from 3.33% to 2.50% and from 5.00% to 3.33%, respectively. The 4B warmup setting starts from a stronger SFT student and achieves the best final average accuracy (16.38%), exceeding the corresponding Base-initialized OPD setting by 6.22 points. In the 4B masking setting, accuracy improves even though only approximately 10% of the sampled responses retain nonzero loss after abnormal responses are masked.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Distillation paradigms and capability transfer. Knowledge distillation matches teacher distributions ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) or trains on teacher sequences ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) ; for reasoning models, the supervision is teacher rationales and trajectories ( Ho et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ; Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Mitra et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , which extend coverage beyond the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . OPD instead supervises student-generated trajectories at student-visited states ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , with extensions to self-distillation ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026b ) , representation-level supervision ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , multiple teachers ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Kimi Team et al., 2026 ) , and cross-tokenizer transfer ( He et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . These broaden teacher supervision but retain the reliance on student rollouts, over which our runs mainly redistribute probability rather than expanding the student’s observed solvable set. Failure modes and stabilization of OPD. OPD failures arise from mismatches among student rollouts, teacher supervision, and token-level objectives. Li et al. (2026) show that a stronger teacher need not help under reasoning-pattern mismatch; Fu et al. (2026) and Zhu et al. (2026) identify unreliable guidance on student prefixes and bias from approximate reverse-KL updates. Remedies include off-policy warm starts, data selection, stop-gradient objectives, trust regions ( Xing et al., 2026 ) , and prefix correction ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Rollout-signal feedback creates another failure class: Wang et al. (2026b) identify signal-correctness mismatch and length exploitation, while Luo et al. (2026) link length inflation to truncation and repetition collapse, motivating clipping, reference regularization, rollout mixing, and length control ( He et al., 2026a ; Heo et al., 2026 ) . We instead view OPD as selecting among student-accessible behaviors by teacher preference, and analyze how biases in that preference affect training. Rollout pathologies in on-policy post-training. On-policy optimization trains only on trajectories sampled from the current model and is therefore exposed to the pathologies of its own rollout distribution. For RLVR, pass@k and likelihood analyses show that training mainly redistributes probability over solution paths already accessible to the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) , and related studies find that reinforcement learning can amplify behaviors acquired during pretraining ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and reduce the diversity of reasoning trajectories ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . Rollouts can further carry degenerate patterns such as malformed formats, excessive length, truncation, and self-reinforcing repetition. Repetition can be reinforced by token co-occurrence effects ( Yan et al., 2024 ) , while RLVR systems counter rollout pathologies with format rewards ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , length-debiased advantage estimation ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , and dynamic sampling with overlong filtering ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . OPD inherits this dependence on student rollouts but evaluates them through a teacher-derived signal; we show that degenerate student behaviors can bias the induced preference itself and thereby become preferentially retained during training.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We interpret on-policy distillation as an RL-like process in which the teacher acts as an implicit reward model for the student’s own responses. Across our experiments on competition mathematics, OPD improves sampling efficiency without expanding the observed solvable set. Its gains primarily come from making correct responses already accessible to the initial student easier to sample. This view also helps explain why OPD can collapse despite normal convergence. In the collapsed setting, the student increasingly follows the teacher’s preferences while producing longer and more repetitive responses. These responses receive high teacher advantage even before training, although the teacher rarely generates them itself. Masking the loss on truncated responses and initializing the student from an SFT checkpoint mitigate this failure while keeping the teacher fixed.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Computational constraints limit our experiments to small models and mathematical reasoning tasks, where prior work has reported clear cases of OPD success and collapse. Whether our findings extend to larger models or other domains remains to be studied. Our interventions are designed specifically to address the overlong and repetitive generations observed in our experiments. We use them mainly to test our explanation of OPD collapse, rather than propose them as general solutions for OPD training. Finally, our coverage results are based on a finite number of samples. Although we use additional sampling and manual inspection to check apparently new solutions, we cannot rule out that larger sampling budgets or different decoding settings would uncover additional correct responses from the initial model.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work studies the reasoning behavior and training dynamics of language models using publicly available models and mathematical reasoning datasets. We do not identify ethical concerns specific to the experiments presented here beyond those associated with the underlying models and datasets.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: All models and datasets used in this work are publicly available, either through open releases or accompanying prior publications. The appendix describes the training configurations, evaluation protocols, and analysis procedures. We plan to release all evaluation and analysis scripts to facilitate reproduction of our results.

sections.heading: A.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We use two evaluation protocols, and they differ only in how many responses are drawn per problem. Both sample at top- p p 1.0 1.0 , use the same generation length limit as training, and serialize prompts with the template described in Appendix A.4 . The sampling temperature follows the model being evaluated rather than the protocol. In the JustRL setting and the DeepScaleR setting, S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} and S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} are both sampled at T = 1.0 T=1.0 , matching the rollout temperature used in training.

sections.heading: Routine evaluation.
sections.text: Endpoint and per-checkpoint accuracies are reported as mean@4: we draw four responses per problem, and calculate average accuracy among all the responses. This protocol is used for the accuracy columns in Section 5.2 and for the accuracy traces over training.

sections.heading: Large-pool evaluation.
sections.text: The coverage and pass @k analyses in Section 3 require a much larger budget. For each model and each of the 90 AIME24–26 problems we draw n = 256 n=256 responses. This pool supports pass @k for k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } k\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\} and the per-problem success rate p ^ m ​ ( q ) \hat{p}_{m}(q) , defined as the fraction of verifier-correct responses among the 256 samples.

sections.heading: Conditional extension for the coverage audit.
sections.text: For the audit in Appendix B we extend sampling only where it can change the conclusion. For every problem covered by S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} but not by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} at n = 256 n=256 , we draw a further 768 responses from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} , giving a conditional pool of 1,024 responses for that problem. The prompt, temperature, top- p p , and length limit are unchanged; only the number of samples increases.

sections.heading: The audit protocol is deliberately one-sided.
sections.text: Both halves of the audit act in a single direction, and we state this explicitly rather than leave it to be inferred. The additional sampling is spent only on problems that S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} covers and S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} does not; the reverse case—covered by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} but not by S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} —never receives a larger S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} pool. Manual review is applied to the same candidate list, where it reinstates verifier misses among S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses and rejects invalid S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} derivations. Relative to the unaudited 256-response pools, the procedure can therefore only raise S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} coverage and only lower S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} coverage, which is the direction that favors the conclusion of Section 3 . We chose this design because a symmetric audit at equal budget would spend most of it on problems whose status is not in question, and because the claim under test is one-sided: a single surviving S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only problem would refute it, whereas additional S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} -only problems would not change it. The cost is that the audited partition in Table 6 is not a symmetric measurement of the two models. It should be read as an upper bound on S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} coverage and a lower bound on S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} coverage under this protocol, so the empty S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only column reports that no candidate survived a search directed against it, not that the two supports were compared on equal terms. The audited S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} and S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} totals are therefore not on the same footing, and their difference overstates the true gap. A second consequence is that the candidate list differs between the two teacher settings, so the two rows of Table 6 audit the same S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} checkpoint under different budgets. We resolve this by reporting a single S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} set: the union of the problems it is found to solve under either audit. This is sound because S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} is one checkpoint drawing on one shared pool of 256 responses per problem, so a solution recovered in one audit is evidence about the checkpoint and not about the teacher it was audited alongside. No counterpart exists on the S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} side, where the two rows are different models. Pooling in this way gives S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} the combined budget of both audits and so widens the asymmetry above; it cannot create an S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only problem, since enlarging S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} can only remove entries from that column.

sections.heading: Estimating pass @k.
sections.text: Reporting pass @k from a single group of k k responses is high variance. For a problem with c c correct responses among n n , we instead use the standard unbiased estimator of the probability that a group of k k responses drawn without replacement from the pool contains at least one correct response [ Chen et al., 2021 ] , pass ​ @ ​ k = 𝔼 q ​ [ 1 − ( n − c q k ) ( n k ) ] , \textsc{pass}@k=\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c_{q}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right], (5) evaluated at n = 256 n=256 and averaged over problems with equal weight. We compute the ratio as ∏ i = 0 k − 1 ( n − c q − i ) / ( n − i ) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(n-c_{q}-i)/(n-i) to avoid large binomial coefficients. At k = n k=n the estimator reduces to an indicator of whether the pool contains any correct response, so pass @256 equals the observed coverage of that pool.

sections.heading: Correctness.
sections.text: Correctness is always recomputed from the response text; we do not reuse the reward labels stored during rollout, which are produced by a different scorer and under a different generation setting. All three benchmarks have non-negative integer answers, and the verifier extracts a predicted integer with the first rule that applies: the content of the last \boxed{...} holding an integer; otherwise the last integer introduced by an explicit answer cue such as final answer is ; otherwise the response as a whole, if it consists of a single integer. A response with no extractable integer counts as incorrect. Prediction and reference are compared after integer normalization, so the verifier accepts no symbolic equivalence beyond leading-zero and whitespace differences. The second and third rules make the verifier permissive: a response can be scored correct without ever emitting a boxed answer. This matters for the coverage audit, where accepting an accidental hit from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} would weaken the claim it supports. We therefore inspect every S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} recovery found in the extended pools by hand rather than trusting the verifier alone, and report the outcome per problem in Appendix B .

sections.heading: A.4 Prompt Templates
sections.text: Training and evaluation examples contain one user message and no system message. Each training example already includes the instruction Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed {}. after the problem statement, separated by a newline in DeepMath and a space in OpenThoughts3. We include the same instruction for mathematics evaluation and serialize the message with the student’s chat template. Routine evaluation uses the same template as training. Below, {QUESTION} denotes the problem statement without this instruction.

sections.heading: JustRL and DeepScaleR settings.
sections.text: Both use the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B student template: JustRL / DeepScaleR Prompt | DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B <｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>{QUESTION} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.<｜Assistant｜><think> The assistant prefix ends with <think> followed by a newline, leaving the reasoning block open for generation.

sections.heading: Qwen3-4B setting.
sections.text: We use the Qwen3-1.7B student template with thinking mode disabled. Specifically, we prefill the assistant turn with an empty reasoning block, <think> followed by two newlines, </think> , and two more newlines. Generation therefore starts after the closed block. The serialized prompt is: Qwen3-4B Setting Prompt | Qwen3-1.7B | Thinking Disabled <|im_start|>user {QUESTION} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> </think> Disabling thinking mode changes this assistant prefix; the user instruction to reason step by step remains in the prompt.

sections.heading: Teacher scoring.
sections.text: After the student generates a response, we feed the full token sequence—the serialized prompt and the student-generated response—into the teacher in a single forward pass to obtain the next-token distributions at the response positions for distillation. The teacher generates no new tokens ( max_new_tokens=0 ). We use the student’s original token sequence directly, without reapplying a chat template or adding any instructions.

sections.heading: Appendix F Training Details for the Candidate-Pool Interventions
sections.text: Section 5.2 compares three Qwen3-4B teacher settings. The baseline and masked settings initialize the student from Qwen3-1.7B-Base. The warmup setting instead initializes it from the Qwen3-1.7B-SFT checkpoint released by Li et al. [2026] and uses that model as the fixed reference. All three use OpenThoughts3 prompts, temperature 1.0 1.0 , an 8,192-token generation length limit, and the optimization settings in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: Loss masking for truncated or failed responses.
sections.text: The baseline trains on all sampled responses, including those that reach the generation length limit. In the masked setting, we set the loss mask to zero for truncated or failed responses; completed responses retain nonzero loss masks and contribute to training. Truncated or failed responses remain in reward and advantage normalization but contribute no policy, reference-KL, or entropy gradient. The loss is first averaged over unmasked response tokens within each sample and then over samples in the global batch.

sections.heading: Initialization from a released SFT checkpoint.
sections.text: The warmup setting directly loads the Qwen3-1.7B-SFT checkpoint released by Li et al. [2026] ; we do not perform an additional SFT stage ourselves. Its higher initial accuracy is part of the intervention: it tests whether supplying a better initial candidate pool changes what OPD can amplify.

Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) has become an important approach to language model post-training. However, despite its performance gains, OPD can also collapse into excessively long and repetitive generation, and the mechanism underlying these divergent outcomes remains poorly understood. We explain these outcomes through a reinforcement learning perspective: the teacher implicitly rewards student behaviors, even those it rarely exhibits itself. From this perspective, our experiments show that OPD improves performance without expanding the student’s capabilities. When the implicit reward model is reliable, OPD makes correct responses easier to sample. In contrast, when the preference misaligns with quality, reward hacking happens: the implicit reward model amplifies overlong, repetitive student rollouts, even though it rarely generates such text itself. Guided by this diagnosis, we find that masking unhealthy responses during training and using SFT initialization can each effectively mitigate the collapse. Together, these findings show that OPD amplifies student behaviors favored by the teacher’s implicit feedback, shifting the focus from how well the teacher generates to how reliably it evaluates student rollouts. The teacher scores student-generated trajectories rather than supplying training trajectories of its own; the examples illustrate how its preferences can amplify either coherent or degenerate student behavior. 1 Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) has become an important approach for developing frontier language models and has been adopted in large-scale post-training pipelines ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ; Kimi Team et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . At each iteration, the current student samples its own responses, and the teacher supervises it through token-level KL divergence at student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . While prior work has demonstrated the potential of OPD to improve student performance, recent studies have reported unstable training and degenerate behaviors, including excessive response length and repetition ( Li et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . It remains unclear what OPD actually learns during training, and why this learning process can sometimes lead to collapse. In this paper, we view OPD from an RL perspective, in which the teacher implicitly rewards the student’s own responses. We investigate OPD on mathematical tasks using different types of teachers, including RL-trained reasoning models and larger general-purpose models. Our experiments show that OPD does not directly extend the student’s capability. Instead, it changes the relative probability of responses the student already produces according to the teacher’s preferences. When these preferences align with response quality, this reweighting can improve sampling efficiency; when they do not, it can lead to reward hacking, with the student increasingly producing responses that receive high implicit rewards despite poor quality. We substantiate this view through three findings. First, we show that successful OPD reinforces correct responses the student can already generate. We compare the initial and trained students across sampling budgets, combining pass@ k k evaluation with additional sampling and manual audits. Although OPD substantially improves single-sample accuracy(pass@1), the gains progressively diminish as the sampling budget increases. At the same time, we find no expansion of the observed solvable set: problems solved after OPD can also be solved by the initial student given sufficient sampling. Together, these results suggest that OPD makes existing capabilities easier to elicit rather than expanding the student model’s problem-solving capabilities. In contrast, we find that the observed OPD collapse reflects reward hacking: training reinforces poor-quality responses favored by the teacher. We compare a successful OPD run with a reproduction of the collapsed setting reported by Li et al. (2026) . Despite their sharply different outcomes, both runs converge normally and concentrate on responses with low negative log-likelihood under the initial student, suggesting that collapse is not simply a failure of optimization or convergence. In the collapsed run, the student produces increasingly overlong and repetitive responses. At the same time, its response distribution shifts markedly toward responses preferred by the teacher over those the teacher disfavors, indicating that the student is fitting the teacher’s preference signal increasingly well. The student thus learns the teacher’s preferences even as its generation quality deteriorates. Building on this diagnosis, we mitigate OPD collapse with a standard remedy for reward hacking: limiting the reinforcement of pathological responses. Before training, higher implicit rewards favor correct and concise responses in the successful setting, but overlong and repetitive responses in the collapsed setting, with both types of behavior later amplified during training. Notably, the teacher itself rarely generates such pathological responses, showing that generation quality does not reliably reflect feedback quality on student rollouts. Keeping the teacher fixed, masking rollouts that reach the generation limit mitigates degeneration and improves average evaluation accuracy by 3.08 percentage points, and SFT warmup provides a complementary solution by improving the quality of the student’s initial rollout distribution. Together, these results show that collapse can be mitigated by controlling which student rollouts are available for reinforcement. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We interpret OPD as an RL-like process with the teacher acting as an implicit reward model, linking its performance gains to improved sampling efficiency. • We identify reward hacking in the observed collapse: the student fits the teacher’s preferences increasingly well even as its generation quality deteriorates. • We trace the collapse to a biased teacher reward signal. Knowledge distillation matches teacher distributions ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) or trains on teacher sequences ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) ; for reasoning models, the supervision is teacher rationales and trajectories ( Ho et al., 2023 ; Hsieh et al., 2023 ; Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Mitra et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , which extend coverage beyond the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . OPD instead supervises student-generated trajectories at student-visited states ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , with extensions to self-distillation ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026b ) , representation-level supervision ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , multiple teachers ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Kimi Team et al., 2026 ) , and cross-tokenizer transfer ( He et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . These broaden teacher supervision but retain the reliance on student rollouts, over which our runs mainly redistribute probability rather than expanding the student’s observed solvable set. Failure modes and stabilization of OPD. OPD failures arise from mismatches among student rollouts, teacher supervision, and token-level objectives. Li et al. (2026) show that a stronger teacher need not help under reasoning-pattern mismatch; Fu et al. (2026) and Zhu et al. (2026) identify unreliable guidance on student prefixes and bias from approximate reverse-KL updates. Remedies include off-policy warm starts, data selection, stop-gradient objectives, trust regions ( Xing et al., 2026 ) , and prefix correction ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Rollout-signal feedback creates another failure class: Wang et al. (2026b) identify signal-correctness mismatch and length exploitation, while Luo et al. (2026) link length inflation to truncation and repetition collapse, motivating clipping, reference regularization, rollout mixing, and length control ( He et al., 2026a ; Heo et al., 2026 ) . We instead view OPD as selecting among student-accessible behaviors by teacher preference, and analyze how biases in that preference affect training. Rollout pathologies in on-policy post-training. On-policy optimization trains only on trajectories sampled from the current model and is therefore exposed to the pathologies of its own rollout distribution. For RLVR, pass@k and likelihood analyses show that training mainly redistributes probability over solution paths already accessible to the base model ( Yue et al., 2025 ) , and related studies find that reinforcement learning can amplify behaviors acquired during pretraining ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and reduce the diversity of reasoning trajectories ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . Rollouts can further carry degenerate patterns such as malformed formats, excessive length, truncation, and self-reinforcing repetition. Repetition can be reinforced by token co-occurrence effects ( Yan et al., 2024 ) , while RLVR systems counter rollout pathologies with format rewards ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , length-debiased advantage estimation ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , and dynamic sampling with overlong filtering ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . OPD inherits this dependence on student rollouts but evaluates them through a teacher-derived signal; we show that degenerate student behaviors can bias the induced preference itself and thereby become preferentially retained during training. 7 Conclusion We interpret on-policy distillation as an RL-like process in which the teacher acts as an implicit reward model for the student’s own responses. Across our experiments on competition mathematics, OPD improves sampling efficiency without expanding the observed solvable set. Its gains primarily come from making correct responses already accessible to the initial student easier to sample. This view also helps explain why OPD can collapse despite normal convergence. In the collapsed setting, the student increasingly follows the teacher’s preferences while producing longer and more repetitive responses. These responses receive high teacher advantage even before training, although the teacher rarely generates them itself. Masking the loss on truncated responses and initializing the student from an SFT checkpoint mitigate this failure while keeping the teacher fixed. Limitations Computational constraints limit our experiments to small models and mathematical reasoning tasks, where prior work has reported clear cases of OPD success and collapse. Whether our findings extend to larger models or other domains remains to be studied. Our interventions are designed specifically to address the overlong and repetitive generations observed in our experiments. Conditional extension for the coverage audit. For the audit in Appendix B we extend sampling only where it can change the conclusion. For every problem covered by S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} but not by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} at n = 256 n=256 , we draw a further 768 responses from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} , giving a conditional pool of 1,024 responses for that problem. The prompt, temperature, top- p p , and length limit are unchanged; only the number of samples increases. The audit protocol is deliberately one-sided. Both halves of the audit act in a single direction, and we state this explicitly rather than leave it to be inferred. The additional sampling is spent only on problems that S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} covers and S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} does not; the reverse case—covered by S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} but not by S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} —never receives a larger S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} pool. Manual review is applied to the same candidate list, where it reinstates verifier misses among S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} responses and rejects invalid S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} derivations. Relative to the unaudited 256-response pools, the procedure can therefore only raise S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} coverage and only lower S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} coverage, which is the direction that favors the conclusion of Section 3 . We chose this design because a symmetric audit at equal budget would spend most of it on problems whose status is not in question, and because the claim under test is one-sided: a single surviving S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only problem would refute it, whereas additional S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} -only problems would not change it. The cost is that the audited partition in Table 6 is not a symmetric measurement of the two models. It should be read as an upper bound on S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} coverage and a lower bound on S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} coverage under this protocol, so the empty S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only column reports that no candidate survived a search directed against it, not that the two supports were compared on equal terms. The audited S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} and S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} totals are therefore not on the same footing, and their difference overstates the true gap. A second consequence is that the candidate list differs between the two teacher settings, so the two rows of Table 6 audit the same S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} checkpoint under different budgets. We resolve this by reporting a single S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} set: the union of the problems it is found to solve under either audit. This is sound because S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} is one checkpoint drawing on one shared pool of 256 responses per problem, so a solution recovered in one audit is evidence about the checkpoint and not about the teacher it was audited alongside. No counterpart exists on the S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} side, where the two rows are different models. Pooling in this way gives S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} the combined budget of both audits and so widens the asymmetry above; it cannot create an S OPD S_{\mathrm{OPD}} -only problem, since enlarging S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} can only remove entries from that column. Correctness is always recomputed from the response text; we do not reuse the reward labels stored during rollout, which are produced by a different scorer and under a different generation setting. All three benchmarks have non-negative integer answers, and the verifier extracts a predicted integer with the first rule that applies: the content of the last \boxed{...} holding an integer; otherwise the last integer introduced by an explicit answer cue such as final answer is ; otherwise the response as a whole, if it consists of a single integer. A response with no extractable integer counts as incorrect. Prediction and reference are compared after integer normalization, so the verifier accepts no symbolic equivalence beyond leading-zero and whitespace differences. The second and third rules make the verifier permissive: a response can be scored correct without ever emitting a boxed answer. This matters for the coverage audit, where accepting an accidental hit from S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} would weaken the claim it supports. We therefore inspect every S INIT S_{\mathrm{INIT}} recovery found in the extended pools by hand rather than trusting the verifier alone, and report the outcome per problem in Appendix B .
